Our office has this one email thread that everyone gets added to eventually, some old distribution list that apparently still includes literally every employee across three different office locations, a fact almost nobody remembered until that day.
A coworker sent out a mildly funny meme to a small group of us.
It poked fun at our team's obsession with a specific printer that jams roughly every other day without fail.
I hit reply and added my own joke about that same printer.
I felt pretty proud of my contribution to what I assumed was still a small, private little thread among four or five people, exactly the way it had always been.
Except, somehow, that original small thread had accidentally been sent to the giant company-wide list instead.
My printer joke had just landed in the inbox of every single employee at the company.
I didn't realize any of this until my phone started buzzing nonstop, notification after notification, way more than a normal work email should ever generate in under a minute.
Within minutes, replies started flooding in.

Some people laughed along and added their own printer complaints, while others, apparently unfamiliar with our printer's reputation, seemed genuinely confused about what was even happening and started asking who I even was.
Someone from a completely different department, one I'd never even met, replied all asking to be removed from the thread.
That message, of course, also went out to the entire company, doubling the confusion instantly.
That single request kicked off an absolute avalanche.
Dozens of people replied all asking to be removed, and each one landed in everyone's inbox, creating this ridiculous chain reaction that lasted almost an entire hour.
At one point, someone even replied all just to complain about all the other reply-alls.
That, of course, generated its own wave of replies, turning the whole thing into a self-sustaining chaos machine.
IT eventually had to step in and manually shut the whole thread down.

They sent out one final company-wide email apologizing for the chaos and reminding everyone, very directly, how the "reply all" button actually works, complete with a screenshot for anyone still confused.
Now, our team has a private, tightly monitored group chat exclusively for printer complaints.
I still get the occasional message from a stranger in another department, just to say the printer joke was genuinely worth it.

Someone even made a small plaque for the actual printer itself, jokingly labeling it "the printer that broke the company email," and it now sits right next to it, permanently, as a kind of office legend.
